2026-118 This authorizes the acceptance and expenditure of a 2027 High Visibility 
Enforcement grant from the Maine Bureau of Highway Safety for several traffic safety 
initiatives, as follows: (1) $4,759.60 for Drug Recognition Expert and Forensic 
Phlebotomist training and callouts, (2) $6,234 for NHTSA impaired driving campaigns 
with Drive Sober Maine and the Regional Impaired Driving Enforcement (RIDE) team, 
(3) $12,468 for speed and aggressive driving enforcement, (4) $10,390 for 
pedestrian/motor vehicle traffic enforcement, and (5) $6,500 for Crash 
Reconstructionist training. The acceptance and expenditure of these grant funds are 
supported by the Administration, received first reading on October 19, 2026, and are 
in order for final Council action.  
 
2026-119 This authorizes the City to enter into an easement agreement with the Portland Water 
District (PWD) to allow the City access to and across PWD property located at 41 
Brown Street to complete the replacement of a failing box culvert. The culvert goes 
from the PWD property across Brown Street and into the Presumpscot River, and this 
easement will accommodate the installation and future maintenance of the new 
culvert. This easement is supported by the Administration, received first reading on 
October 19, 2026, and is in order for final Council action. 
 
2026-120 This is a PUBLIC HEARING on an amendment to the Land Use Ordinance Section 335-
1.8, Definitions, Section 335-2.9.1, Data Centers  (new), and Section 335-6.12.B, 
Contract Zone 12, Rock Row Contract Zone Permitted Uses, relating to Data Centers. 
The City Council adopted Order 2026-66 on June 1, 2026, Adopting a Data Center 
Moratorium Ordinance. This action established a 180-day moratorium on new data 
center projects while referring this item to the Planning Board to study and review 
existing ordinance language and to provide a recommendation on whether any 
enhanced or limited standards should be incorporated into the Land Use Ordinance. 
The Planning Board held a workshop on September 1, 2026 and a Public Hearing on 
October 6, 2026, after which they unanimously approved a recommendation to the 
City Council to amend the Land Use Ordinance to (1) update the definition of Data 
Centers, (2) establish a new section stating that Data Centers may only be permitted

as an Accessory Use, and (3) eliminating Data Centers as a permitted use within the 
Rock Row Contract Zone, which is the only place that Data Centers are currently 
permitted within the Land Use Ordinance. Director of Planning & Code Enforcement

of the public hearing was posted in City Hall and on the City’s website, and was 
published in the Portland Press Herald on Friday, October 23, 2026. This Land Use 
Ordinance amendment is supported by the Administration, received first reading on 
October 19, 2026, and, following public hearing, is in order for final Council action.

2026-121 This authorizes the Mayor or designee to enter into a retainer agreement with 
Gustafson Gluek, PLLC of Minneapolis, MN to represent the City of Westbrook as part 
of the indirect purchaser class action lawsuit brought against several fire apparatus 
manufacturers, including REV Group, LLC, Oshkosh Corporation, Pierce 
Manufacturing, Inc., and Rosenbauer America, LLC, and the Fire Apparatus 
Manufacturers’ Association. There are two pending class action lawsuits against 
these defendants, one filed by direct purchasers and the other filed by indirect 
purchasers, which includes those who purchased apparatus through a distributor, 
as Westbrook did. Both classes assert that the manufacturers artificially inflated 
costs, forced production delays, applied retroactive price hikes, and further allege 
that FAMA facilitated the sharing of economic data between manufacturers. As 
outlined in the enclosed memo from Fire Chief Steve Sloan, the City of Westbrook 
purchased a Quint Ladder Truck from E-One, a subsidiary of REV Group, LLC in 2021. 
The City experienced delivery delays, adjustments to final price, and a performance 
guarantee was withheld due to claimed manufacturer delays.

A federal district court judge in Wisconsin appointed Preti Flaherty (City Solicitor) as 
one of four co-lead firms on behalf of the direct purchaser class (those who 
purchased apparatus directly from the manufacturer). The indirect purchaser class 
(those who purchased through a dealer) is represented in part by Gustafson Gluek of 
Minneapolis, MN. This agreement will allow the City of Westbrook to participate in 
the indirect purchaser class action litigation. While class action litigation may take 
several years to reach conclusion, there are no upfront or separate out-of-pocket 
obligations for attorney fees, as fees and expenses are contingent upon and payable 
from any recovery under the agreement. Authorization of this agreement is supported 
by the Administration and is in order for final Council action.

2026-122 This authorizes the Mayor or designee sell the City-owned property at 12 Water Street 
to Dori Schulberger of Westbrook, ME for not less than $50,000. It also authorizes the 
Mayor or designee to negotiate and enter into a Purchase & Sale Agreement for the 
sale of the property and to execute a deed and other documents necessary to sell the 
property. The City of Westbrook acquired several parcels along the northern side of 
the Presumpscot River from Sappi in April 2023, which included the land addressed 
as 12 Water Street. Following the acquisition, the City was contacted by Dori 
Schulberger alerting staff to her residence on the property and her family’s history. 
Her mother, Sharon Schulberger, obtained a lease agreement for the parcel from 
Scott Paper Company in 1980 and located a mobile home and later a shed on the 
property. The original lease terms outlined rent at a cost of $300/yr, though at some 
later date this was increased to $400/yr. Later, SD Warren assumed the lease and 
continued to honor the existing terms. Following the passing of Ms. Sharon 
Schulberger, her daughter (Ms. Dori Schulberger) assumed the lease and continued 
the annual rent payment of $400/yr to Sappi, and later to the City of Westbrook after 
the City acquired the property. Ms. Schulberger approached the City asking for 
permission to purchase the parcel. An appraisal of the property valued the parcel at 
$50,000, given site unique conditions and limited buildable space on the parcel 
combined with the construction easements and other conditions that the City would 
retain upon sale. Ms. Schulberger is obtaining a formal survey of the property at her 
own cost. This order authorizes the Mayor or designee to execute a Purchase & Sale 
Agreement and sell the property at the proposed price and subject to such other 
terms and conditions as the Mayor or designee deems in the City’s interests. The 
$50,000 in revenue would be assigned to the Riverwalk North Project. This property 
sale is supported by the Administration and is in order for first reading. 
 
2026-123 This approves the 2026-2029 Collective Bargaining Agreement between the City of 
Westbrook and the Westbrook Essential Services Unit (ESU). This unit was 
established to separate twelve (12) positions from the existing General Unit, and to 
recognize them as a distinct bargaining unit represented by Teamsters Local Union 
Page 6 of 144
No. 340. This change provided an opportunity to develop a collective bargaining 
agreement that more appropriately addresses the compensation, benefits, and 
working conditions of these employees. This agreement defines “essential services 
employees” as those whose primary duties are necessary to maintain the continuity 
of critical municipal operations, public infrastructure, including but not limited to 
maintenance, operational, facilities, wastewater, grounds, and administrative 
support functions essential to City services, but excludes certain positions that are 
either per diem, seasonal, part-time, non-union, or otherwise excluded by law or 
included in another City union. In March 2026, the City and Union filed the necessary 
documentation with the Maine Labor Relations Board to formalize the removal of 
these positions from the General Unit and their placement into the newly established 
Essential Services Unit. The filing was accepted by the Board, formalizing the change 
in bargaining unit representation.  
 
As a starting point for the new unit, the City and the Union used the existing General 
Unit collective bargaining agreement as a template, providing a consistent 
foundation for contract language, benefits, and working conditions while allowing for 
provisions specific to the Essential Services Unit. A significant component of the 
agreement is the implementation of a new pay scale effective July 1, 2026, developed 
using salary market data obtained from area municipalities. Individual wage 
increases vary based on each position's placement on the new pay scale and the 
corresponding market data, with an average increase of approximately 5% across the 
unit to reflect market salary rates. Additional provisions include the following:  
• Annual Wage Adjustments: A 3% cost-of-living adjustment effective July 1, 
2027 and July 1, 2028. 
• Signing Bonus: A one-time $500 signing bonus for each of the 12 bargaining-
unit members following settlement and ratification of the agreement. 
• Benefits and Working Conditions: Updates to reflect current City practices, 
changes in applicable law, and organizational changes, including revisions to 
overtime, vacation and sick leave, clothing allowances, education 
reimbursement, and Maine Paid Family Medical Leave.  
 
The projected costs associated with the new pay scale, signing bonus, and 
negotiated wage adjustments are $51,375.31 in Year 1 (July 1, 2026 – June 30, 2027, 
includes $45,375.31 for the establishment of a new pay scale and $6,000 for the one-
time signing bonus), $27,813.87 in Year 2 (July 1, 2027 – June 30, 2028), and 
$28,648.28 in Year 3 (July 1, 2028 – June 30, 2029), for an estimated cumulative cost 
of $107,837.46 for this three-year contract, excluding scheduled step increases and 
any additional costs associated with other agreement provisions. The terms of this 
agreement were ratified by a vote of the union membership. This agreement is 
supported by the Administration and is in order for first reading.

The municipal assessments associated with Metro’s FY 2027 are drawn from the municipalities’

officers” (i.e., the city/town councils) of your communities  are required to notify Metro of a

The budget is organized into three major operational sections:  
 
• Base Bus Service – $22.2 million budget represents a 14.5% increase compared to 2026. 
The increase is primarily being driven by wage/benefits and the rising cost of fuel.  
Metro plans to operate 160,159 hours of transit service across 15  fixed routes and two 
microtransit zones in 2027. Ridership in 2026 is projected to reach 1.89M, 0.6% increase 
from Metro’s 2025 ridership. Metro is budgeting for ridership to increase by 7% in 2027. 
Growth in ridership is largely projected based on new service in Scarborough and planned 
service improvements in South Portland. Additionally , Metro will be redoubling its 
marketing efforts, including promotion of our new “Tap to Ride” fare option introduced 
in 2026, and Metro Connect on-demand service in Scarborough and Falmouth. 
• ADA Paratransit  – $794k budget represents a 11.2% increase compared to 202 6. 
Increases in ADA paratransit ridership coupled with an increase in Metro’s contract rate 
with its paratransit provider the Regional Transportation Program (RTP) are driving this 
increase.  
 
ADA paratransit service is demand-response service for individuals who  cannot use bus 
service. Passengers may be certified as ADA eligible if a functional assessment determines 
they are unable to use the fixed route bus system for all travel or certain trip types. ADA

• Metro is experiencing two primary revenue challenges; most impactfully the phasing out 
of ARPA funding coupled with increases in federal funding that are not keeping pace with 
escalating expenses . Additionally, state funding is flat, creating a reduction i n the 
percentage of expenses funded by MaineDOT. For its part , Metro raised fares in August 
2026. This increase is expected to boost fare revenue by 9% ; however, this increase in 
fare revenue will not be enough to offset the large reduction in ARPA funding and lack of 
other new funding sources. These factors combined cause overall municipal contributions 
to the budget to increase. The impact of this increase has the most significant impact on 
the communities with ARPA funded service improvements. These ARPA  funded service

o Falmouth – Increased frequency on the Route 7 and the introduction of Metro 
Connect microtransit service to most of Falmouth. 
o Portland – Extension of the Route 7 to the Jetport and frequency improvements

Husky Line to the Eastern Waterfront, and frequency improvements midday on 
the Breez service. 
o Brunswick, Freeport, Yarmouth – Improved frequency midday on the Breez, which 
serves all three communities. 
 
• In 202 6, approximately $544k in service improvements were 100% ARPA funded.

SUMMARY: 
On June 1st the Westbrook City Council adopted an 180-day moratorium on new data center 
projects while referring this item to the Planning Board to study and review Westbrook’s existing 
ordinance language/allowances and provide a recommendation to Council on whether any 
enhanced or limited standards should be incorporated into our Ordinance.  
 
 
Currently, Data Centers are a defined use and are only permitted within Contract Zone 12 (Rock 
Row Contract Zone). The Planning Board reviewed differing types and sizes of Data Centers as 
well as potential opportunities and negative impacts of Data Centers, specifically as it relates to 
water use/discharge, energy demands, noise and economic development. The Board also 
discussed potential regulations that would be more appropriate at a State level and regulatory 
strategies that have been implemented in other areas where growth of Data Centers is more 
prominent.  
Following their September workshop, the Planning Board is recommending a prohibition on 
Data Centers as a principal use. This will allow for accessory Data Centers to remain where the 
Data Center is serving an on-premises legal principal use (ex: server rooms). Staff provided the 
Board with draft language that clarifies the definition of Data Centers, specifically permits them 
only as accessory and removes the use from Contract Zone 12. This item will require a public 
hearing to be held prior to second reading in November.  
The Planning Board held a workshop on September 1, 2026 and a Public Hearing on 
October 6, 2026. At their October meeting the Board provided a unanimous 
recommendation to the City Council for adoption of the amendment.

safe service life.

prices,” where manufacturers raise the final cost of trucks already in production.  
• Alleged conspiracy: FAMA is alleged to have facilitated the sharing of competitive 
economic data between manufacturers, enabling coordination of price increases and 
production slowdowns.

essential emergency equipment and delaying delivery of vehicles critical to public safety.

ARTICLE 26 - STORM & EMERGENCY POLICY  
          
The business of the City of Westbrook requires continuing operations during all except 
extreme conditions, although the safety of employees remains a primary consideration. City 
government will remain open for business as scheduled, except in situations where 
emergency conditions, such as severe inclement weather, natural disasters, public 
disasters, or energy system failures, warrant closing or rescheduling.   
 
Only the Mayor’s Office of the Mayor has the authority to make decisions concerning closure 
of municipal buildings and operations. During an official closing, all  Unit employees, except 
those who are defined as “emergency essential,” will be requested to leave work, if they are 
already present, or not to report for work.  
 
Emergency essential employees are those whose duties and responsibilities are essential 
in carrying out critical operational or life safety services of the City.  General Unit employees 
in the public safety and public services divisions, as well as other positions in the General

Page 40

Unit who serve essential business or support functions, shall be designated as “emergency 
essential.” 
 
“Emergency essential” personnel can vary depending on the nature of the emergency, but 
include the following General Unit positions:   
 
Public Safety Office Coordinator 
Records Administrative Assistant 
Public Services Administrative Assistant 
Sustainability Coordinator 
Operations Supervisor  
Building Superintendent 
Assistant Code Enforcement Officer 
Outdoor Facility & Grounds Superintendent 
Assistant Outdoor Facility & Grounds Superintendent 
Fields Technician 
 
All emergency essential employees will be required to report to work during the closing of 
Westbrook municipal offices if they were previously scheduled to work that day; and they 
also may be called by their supervisor to report on a day off. 
   
Absent a notice of closing from the Mayor’s Office, each City department is expected to 
maintain a normal schedule, whether during a snowstorm, other inclement weather, or 
emergency. Individual departments will not make decisions regarding closure, early 
release, or delay in opening .  The supervisors in each department and division are 
responsible for developing an internal communication mechanism to aid in communicating 
closure of municipal operations from the Mayor’s Office to employees. 
 
During a closing declared by the Mayor’s Office, full -time employees , who are not 
emergency essential, will be compensated at their normal rate for the time they would have 
been scheduled to work. In the case of a late start or early closure, the employee must have 
reported to work to be eligible for compensation for the remainder of the day . For example, 
if municipal operations close at 3  p.m., non-essential employees leaving at that time from 
City Hall positions would also be compensated for the remainder of their normally 
scheduled workday, until 5 p.m. If the City closes for a full day, employees will be 
compensated for that day at their normal rate of pay, to a maximum of eight hours. Essential 
workers who are scheduled to work, and who do work that day, will receive their normal pay 
for that period, without additional premium pay or compensating time off . Part-time 
employees, who are not emergency essential, will be compensated at their normal pay rate 
only if they were scheduled to work that day, and only for the hours scheduled to work.  
 
During inclement weather, individuals are urged to exercise discretion and sound judgment 
regarding travel, since safe transportation to and from work depends on many factors, such 
as distance and specific road conditions in home areas . When an employee is concerned

that the weather or emergency is potentially severe, and that customer service and/or other 
operations of the department will not be adversely impacted.  
 
In those situations in which a Westbrook Essential Services Unit employee does not report 
or has left early, with the prior approval of the Department Hhead, or their designee, that 
supervisorthey have  has the discretion, based on the nature of the hazard, to allow an

during the same work week. Otherwise, if the employee is unable to make up the full day of

An employee who does not report to work on time, or who leaves early, without prior 
approval by their Department Head, or their designee, may be subject to disciplinary action.  
 
As stated above, the fact that an employee is required to work during emergency conditions
